hero.eyebrow: Musical dyslexia · not officially diagnosed, but real
hero.subheading: The notes are right there on the page. So why won't they hold still?
hero.dek: Dysmusia is a persistent difficulty reading, learning, or recognizing music — present since childhood, unrelated to effort or intelligence. It isn't an official diagnosis yet, but it's a real, recognizable pattern with a name and a growing body of research behind it.
hero.calloutText: Struggling to read music does not mean struggling to understand or make it. Some of the most accomplished musicians in history have worked almost entirely by ear.

ways.heading: Four ways in, when reading alone doesn't work
ways.intro: Multisensory instruction is well established for language-based dyslexia. The same logic applies to music: route the same information through more than one sense at once.

items.title: Visual
items.body: Color-coded notes and staff positions turn an abstract symbol into a pattern the eye catches quickly.

items.title: Auditory
items.body: Listening to a phrase before reading it gives the ear a target to match the page against.

items.title: Kinesthetic
items.body: Walking a floor staff, hand-signing pitch, or tracing notation adds movement and touch to the memory.

items.title: Imagination
items.body: A short mnemonic or character gives working memory something more durable than an abstract mark.

research.heading: The research is real, but still thin.
research.body: There isn't yet a large body of research specifically on music-reading difficulty, especially compared to dyslexia. What exists — from congenital amusia research to specialist case studies — suggests a real relationship worth taking seriously, alongside promising evidence that multisensory teaching helps.
